To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
expiratory loss of water from the respiratory tract is not the cause of the decrease in lung functions seen after hyperventilation.

1) expiratory water losses are not the cause of the decreased lung function seen after exercise in asthmatics, 2) the water loss in the respiratory tract during exercise in asthmatic patients is similar to that of healthy subjects, 3) exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is caused by a combination of factors including hyperventilation and water loss, and 4) the water loss from the respiratory mucosa is not a major factor in causing the decrease in lung volumes
In summary, our research is concerned with
water loss from the respiratory system during hyperventillation.
the effects of hyperventilation on the lung function of normal subjects and asthmatics.
water loss from the respiratory system and its possible effect on the airways in asthmatics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the expiratory water losses in the asthmatic and healthy individuals are similar, and that the decrease in PEF seen in the asthmactic patients after hyperventilation is not due to water loss from the airway.
there is no evidence that expiratory airway cooling and water loss are important factors in exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
water loss from the respiratory mucosa during exercise in asthmatic subjects is not the main cause of the decrease in lung functions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the water loss from the respiratory system is small and is of no importance to the lung function in healthy subjects.
the decrease in PEF after exercise and hypoventilation is caused by an increased bronchial reactivity to histamine and/or a decreased bronchial reactivitiy to beta-agonist.
we have shown that there is no difference in water loss from the respiratory system between asthmatics and healthy subjects during hyperventillation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the water loss per se does not seem to be the reason for the decreased lung function seen in the asthmatic group.
the use of a simple water loss test is not a useful tool in the diagnosis of exercise induced bronchospasm.
the water loss from the respiratory tracts is not the reason why the PEF decreases in asthmatics.
